extracted.intended_audience: educators, presenters, meeting organizers, researchers, and technologists interested in audience response systems
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical considerations for selecting, deploying, and using audience response systems (hardware- or software-based) in co-located or remote settings, especially for education, conferences, and polling. Covers technical, pedagogical, operational, and data-integration aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for co-located vs remote audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems for co-located audiences combine wireless hardware with presentation software; systems for remote audiences may use telephones or web polls for audiences watching through television or the internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a system whose deployment model matches your setting (in-room wireless keypads and base stations for co-located groups; SMS/HTTP/web polls for remote or broadcast audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware-based vs software/cloud-based solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardware solutions use wireless keypads and receivers; software/cloud solutions allow responses from personal devices such as cell phones, smartphones, and laptops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardware may be necessary where BYOD isn't feasible; cloud/software reduces device inventory but depends on participants' devices and network access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supported question formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Common question types include multiple choice, true/false, numerical answers; more advanced systems support open-ended responses, dial testing, voteable items, short word answers, and free-text that can be aggregated into word clouds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the system's question-format capabilities to your pedagogical or research needs (e.g., need open-ended/word-cloud support for qualitative feedback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity vs ability to track individual responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on requirements, data can either be collected anonymously (e.g., voting) or traced to individual participants (e.g., classroom quizzes, graded activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether anonymity or identifiable tracking is needed; some systems offer both modes and can store per-user data in a database/gradebook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data storage, reporting, and export / LMS/API integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Incoming data may be stored in a database on the host computer; reports can be created after the presentation and data can be loaded manually or via API into learning management systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the system supports saving results, exporting reports, and integrating with your LMS or research workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate aggregation and display of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience Response software collects results and the aggregate data is graphically displayed within the presentation (e.g., bar chart, histogram, worm or trending graph) in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real-time visualization is important for formative feedback and engagement; check how results are displayed and whether correct answers can be indicated immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation for open-ended responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Some services offer presenters real-time moderation for open-ended responses or questions prior to displaying them on screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using free-text inputs in public settings, prefer systems that provide moderation to filter inappropriate or irrelevant content before display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and participant capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: RF systems can accommodate hundreds to thousands of voters (some systems allow multiple base stations to be linked); web-based systems can gather responses at massive scale across sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the system's capacity and networking model to expected audience size and whether multi-site polling is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission technology and constraints (IR, RF, Internet/HTTP, SMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary transmission technologies are infrared (IR), radio frequency (RF), web/Internet (HTTP), and SMS/cell networks; IR requires line-of-sight and suits small groups, RF offers range (300–500 feet) and large group support, web/HTTP enables smartphone/browser voting, and SMS uses telecom infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider room layout, audience size, device availability, and geographic/multi-country issues (SMS hubbing/multi-country limitations) when choosing transmission technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost, procurement, and device lifecycle (purchase price, rental, maintenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The per-unit purchase price of ARS devices can be significantly higher than software-only solutions; maintenance and repair of devices are ongoing costs when devices are owned centrally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for upfront hardware costs, repair/maintenance, potential rentals, and total cost of ownership vs software/BYOD alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configuration, troubleshooting, and support requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: ARS deployment often requires configuration and troubleshooting of presentation software, receivers, and network connectivity; support needs vary by technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure adequate technical support and test-run procedures are in place, especially for live events where failures are disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and performance under room conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance can be affected by room conditions (e.g., IR interference, RF range limits, Wi‑Fi congestion), and hardware may behave poorly under non-optimal conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the target venue (size, wireless environment, line-of-sight) to choose a system tolerant of those conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of hardware-only systems
rubrics_metrics.description: For hardware-only applications there may be a lack of open-ended questions, dial testing capabilities, and other non-standard question formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need open-ended or complex question types, prefer web/app-based systems or hybrid solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: BYOD and smartphone/browser voting support
rubrics_metrics.description: Web-based and smartphone app solutions allow participants to use their own phones or laptops to respond, reducing the need to distribute proprietary hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use BYOD solutions where attendees reliably have compatible devices and network access; consider fallback options where device access is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance, grading, and identity features
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems can track individual responses by linking remotes or accounts to user IDs, enabling attendance verification and grade assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For academic settings where grades or attendance are required, ensure the ARS supports secure user identification and gradebook export.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical impact: improved attentiveness/engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: ARS use tends to increase student engagement and attentiveness (evidence from studies reporting high percentages of faculty and students agreeing that clickers increased engagement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ARS as a tool to promote active learning and maintain attention, particularly in large lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical impact: increased knowledge retention (peer instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer Instruction with ARS (ConcepTests) has been associated with improved student performance and retention compared to traditional instruction in some studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine ARS with pedagogical strategies (peer discussion, follow-up questioning) to maximize learning gains rather than using clickers as a standalone gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative assessment and immediate concept-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: ARS confirms audience understanding of key points immediately, enabling instructors to identify misconceptions and adjust teaching dynamically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short conceptual questions to get instant feedback and adapt instruction in real time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to gather structured data for research and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: AR software records responses to a database, enabling analysis over time and use in educational research or organizational reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If research-quality data is required, verify data export formats, timestamps, participant identifiers (when appropriate), and auditability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with presentation platforms (PowerPoint/Keynote) and visualization types
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ARS products integrate as stand-alone platforms or plug-ins to PowerPoint/Keynote and present results as bar charts, histograms, worms, or word clouds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm seamless integration with your presentation workflow and that visualizations match your communication goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell phone / SMS-specific functionality and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: SMS-based systems collect text inputs and can accept multiple responses per SMS; they avoid dedicated hardware but depend on telecom providers and may have multi-country limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SMS for traveling speakers and large venues without hardware logistics, but check costs, multi-country capability, and features like multi-voting support and text-mining tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: HTTP/web voting and multi-country/multi-network considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: HTTP/browser voting supports apps and browser-based voting and benefits from permanent internet connections on smartphones; SMS remains more penetrant but HTTP supports richer interactions and multi-vote scenarios across borders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For global audiences prefer HTTP/web-based solutions with robust handling of network variability; consider SMS hubbing solutions where HTTP isn't viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Input device completeness and system components
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical ARS components include a base station (receiver), wireless keypads or mobile devices for participants, and ARS software on the presenter's computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your selected system includes all necessary components (receivers, keypads, software) or plan how to provision them.

rubrics_metrics.name: User account and registration workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: In traced modes participants may need to create accounts in advance or remotes may be registered with ID numbers to link responses to identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan user registration and privacy consent processes if identifying participants; streamline account creation for attendees where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement and novelty as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Clickers and ARS can create an interactive and fun learning environment, partly due to novelty and partly because participants are motivated to see results and compare answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in the engagement payoff, but avoid relying solely on novelty — pair ARS with substantive pedagogical design for sustained impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-case fit and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: ARS is used across political campaigns, corporate training, public participation, market research, conferences, game shows, continuing medical education, and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a system whose features (anonymity, scalability, question types, moderation) align with your application's specific needs (e.g., research vs. entertainment vs. graded assessment).
